title: ZOLOFT (sertraline hydrochloride) tablets, for oral use; ZOLOFT (sertraline hydrochloride) oral solution: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration-approved labelling, published in DailyMed (National Library of Medicine); structured product label version 7, published 24 July 2025, label text revised 8/2023; initial US approval 1991
funder: not stated. The document is prescribing information approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and published by the labeller, Viatris Specialty LLC.
result: Indicated for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, social anxiety disorder and premenstrual dysphoric disorder; starting dose 50 mg per day for major depressive disorder, maximum 200 mg per day. Sertraline potentiates serotonergic activity in the central nervous system through inhibition of neuronal reuptake of serotonin; at clinically relevant doses it blocks the uptake of serotonin into human platelets; in vitro studies in animals suggest potent and selective inhibition of neuronal serotonin reuptake with only very weak effects on norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake; no significant affinity for adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopaminergic, histaminergic, serotonergic (5HT1A, 5HT1B, 5HT2) or benzodiazepine receptors; does not inhibit monoamine oxidase. Peak plasma concentrations 4.5 to 8.4 hours after dosing; average terminal elimination half-life about 26 hours; steady state after one week of once-daily dosing; 98% bound to serum proteins. Extensive first-pass metabolism; the principal initial pathway is N-demethylation; N-desmethylsertraline is substantially less active and has a terminal half-life of 62 to 104 hours. Drugs that interfere with serotonin reuptake, including sertraline, increase the risk of bleeding events, and aspirin, NSAIDs, other antiplatelet drugs, warfarin and other anticoagulants may add to this risk. Hyponatraemia may occur with SSRIs and SNRIs; in many cases it appears to result from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; elderly patients, patients taking diuretics and volume-depleted patients may be at greater risk. Adverse reactions after discontinuation, particularly abrupt discontinuation, include nausea, sweating, dysphoric mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, sensory disturbances such as electric shock sensations, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, emotional lability, insomnia, hypomania, tinnitus and seizures; gradual dose reduction rather than abrupt cessation is recommended whenever possible, and patients are advised not to stop abruptly and to discuss any tapering regimen with their healthcare provider. In pooled randomised placebo-controlled trials in 3066 adults exposed to sertraline for 8 to 12 weeks across six indications: nausea 26% against 12% on placebo (n=2293), diarrhoea or loose stools 20% against 10%, ejaculation failure 8% against 1% of men; 368 of 3066 (12%) discontinued for an adverse reaction against 93 of 2293 (4%) on placebo.
